app.name: Sanguine
taglines: The River of Blood never empties; it only crests.
By blood bound, by brass crowned.
Offerings of bone, rivers of red.
The earth drinks deep, yet the Blood God thirsts.
An ocean of red for the Lord of Rage.

how.title: How Sanguine estimates
how.rowDesc: How the ranges are worked out, what the confidence words mean and what changes them.
how.rangeTitle: Where the period range comes from
how.rangeBody: Sanguine looks at the lengths of your last 36 cycles. Before you have logged a few, it starts from published averages for your age group (Bull et al. 2019) and moves towards your own pattern as cycles are added. In most life states, recent cycles and older ones count the same. A cycle that looks like a missed log, or that falls in a life change you set (such as pregnancy, or the months after stopping a hormonal method), is left out or counted less. The result is the range of days that has an 80% likelihood of holding your next period start; the calendar also shows the wider 95% range.

high.rule: At least six cycles and a period range no wider than about a week.

medium.rule: At least two cycles and a period range of up to about 11 days.

low.rule: Fewer than two cycles, or cycles that vary so much the range is wider than about 11 days. The range is wide on purpose.

none.rule: Not enough data yet, or a life change you set pauses the estimates.

how.narrowBody: Logging every period start, including the first day, matters most. Morning temperature, ovulation tests, cervical mucus and cervical position can date ovulation in a cycle after it happens, which sharpens the next period estimate and the fertile window estimate.
how.narrowBodyTeen: Logging every period start, including the first day, matters most. The more cycles you log, the narrower the range becomes.
how.symptomsTitle: What does not change the estimates
how.symptomsBody: Symptoms, mood and notes never change an estimate. They show up in Insights so you can see your own patterns, but there is no published evidence that they predict when a period starts.
how.accuracyTitle: How well it has done for you
how.accuracyBody: When a cycle ends, Sanguine checks whether the range it gives at the start of that cycle, using only what you had logged by then, held the real start date. When an update changes how estimates are worked out, past cycles are checked again the same way. Insights, Your accuracy, shows the count.

draw.blendLabel: With two cycles logged, the estimate still leans on published averages; it moves towards your own pattern as cycles are added, up to your last 36.

draw.narrowLabel: Logging every period start, then morning temperature, ovulation tests, cervical mucus and cervical position, turn a wide range into a narrower one.

guidance.suppCaveat: Supplements are not tested like medicines and can interact with them. A pharmacist or doctor can check one with you before you start, especially if you take other medicines.
guidance.moreA11y: Read the reasons, evidence and sources for these notes

menstrual.food: Iron-rich foods with vitamin C, such as lentil dahl with a squeeze of lemon.
menstrual.move: Any movement that feels good can lift your mood and energy. Rest is fine too.

follicular.food: Vitamin C, B vitamins and zinc, such as muesli with kiwifruit and yoghurt.
follicular.move: Exercise lifts mood and energy. Try harder sessions if you feel up to them.

ovulatory.food: Fibre-rich foods, such as overnight oats with berries.
ovulatory.move: Train as usual, and warm up well before jumping and quick turns.

luteal.food: Protein, magnesium and B12, such as eggs on toast or a handful of almonds.
luteal.move: Keep moving: exercise lifts mood. Drink regularly in warm weather.

premenstrual.food: Calcium-rich foods, such as yoghurt with fruit or a cheese and salad sandwich.
premenstrual.move: A walk, a swim or yoga can lift low mood or energy.

general.food: Iron and calcium: a lentil salad, or yoghurt with fruit.
general.move: Regular activity lifts mood and energy. Even a short walk helps.

guidance.energyLow: In your own logs, your energy was lowest in this part of your cycle. Movement lifts energy for most people, even a short walk.
guidance.caveat: Research on eating and training by cycle phase is young, and how you feel is a better guide than the calendar. This is general information, not medical advice.

evidence.general: General guidance, not specific to this phase

evidenceKey.title: How to read the evidence bars

strong.def: large reviews or national guidelines agree.

some.def: several small trials point the same way, results vary.

early.def: one study, lab work, or a plausible link not tested in people.

general.def: good advice on any day, not specific to this phase.

evidenceKey.note: Estimates use the same bars for confidence: how sure the app is about a date, from your own data.

curve.label: Illustration of a typical cycle: estrogen rises in the first half and again a little after the middle; progesterone rises in the second half; both fall before the next period.
curve.labelHere: You are in this part of the cycle: {phase}.
curve.caption: A typical cycle, drawn to explain. Not your own hormone levels.
curve.captionOwn: Drawn to explain, on the dates of your cycle. A typical pattern, not your own hormone levels.

menstrual.body: Estrogen and progesterone are at their lowest, and bleeding carries iron out of the body. In a study that tracked 397 substances in the blood and urine of 34 women across the cycle, amino acids and vitamin D were higher during the period than in the second half of the cycle.

move.tip: Any movement that feels good, such as a walk, a swim, yoga or your usual training, can lift your mood and energy. Rest is fine too.
move.why: Reviews of more than 1,000 trials find that exercise improves mood and energy, and a single session lifts mood on average. In smaller trials, regular exercise also eased period pain.

menstrual.sources: NHMRC Nutrient Reference Values: iron. Singh and others 2023, British Journal of Sports Medicine. Weinstein and others 2024, Psychosomatic Medicine. Armour and others 2019, Cochrane review of exercise for period pain. Daily and others 2015, Pain Medicine (ginger). 2024 reviews of ginger and of omega-3 for period pain. Hsu and others 2024, Nutrients (zinc). Draper and others 2018, Scientific Reports.

follicular.body: After the period, estrogen rises as a follicle grows in the ovary. In the same study, amino acids and fats in the blood were higher in this phase than in the second half of the cycle.

move.tip: Exercise lifts mood and energy. If you feel energetic, this can be a good time to try harder sessions.
move.why: Reviews of more than 1,000 trials find that exercise improves mood and energy. Performance itself differs little between phases, so let how you feel decide how hard to go.

follicular.sources: NHMRC Nutrient Reference Values (iron, zinc). Chocano-Bedoya and others 2011, American Journal of Clinical Nutrition (B vitamins). Hsu and others 2024, Nutrients (zinc). Singh and others 2023, British Journal of Sports Medicine. Wender and others 2022, Frontiers in Psychology. McNulty and others 2020, Sports Medicine. Draper and others 2018, Scientific Reports.

ovulatory.body: Estrogen peaks and a surge of luteinising hormone triggers ovulation. In the same study, vitamin D and a marker of vitamin B6 were lower around ovulation than during the period.

move.tip: Train as usual, and warm up well before sports with jumping, landing and quick changes of direction.
move.why: Knee ligaments loosen slightly around this time in some studies, but reviews find no phase with clearly more knee injuries. Warm-up programmes halve knee ligament injuries at any time of the cycle.

ovulatory.sources: Draper and others 2018, Scientific Reports. Gaskins and others 2009, American Journal of Clinical Nutrition (fibre). Systematic review of cycle phase and knee injury measures, 2022. Webster and Hewett 2018, Journal of Orthopaedic Research.

luteal.body: Progesterone rises and body temperature goes up by a few tenths of a degree. In the same study, 39 amino acids and 18 fats in the blood were lower in this phase, and so was serotonin, a messenger linked to mood. The authors suggest the body is using the amino acids and fats to build tissue, including the lining of the uterus.

move.tip: Keep moving: exercise lifts mood and energy. In warm weather, drink regularly and give yourself more time to cool down.
move.why: Reviews of more than 1,000 trials find that exercise improves mood, and a single session lifts it on average. Progesterone raises core temperature and the temperature at which sweating starts by about half a degree.

luteal.sources: Draper and others 2018, Scientific Reports. Kriengsinyos and others 2004, American Journal of Physiology. NHMRC Nutrient Reference Values (magnesium, B12). Tucker and others 2024, Nutrition Reviews. Benton and others 2020, PLoS ONE. Singh and others 2023, British Journal of Sports Medicine. Weinstein and others 2024, Psychosomatic Medicine. Gatorade Sports Science Institute review of hydration in active women.

premenstrual.body: Progesterone and estrogen fall in the days before the period. Many women notice lower mood, bloating, cravings or lighter sleep in these days.

move.tip: When your mood or energy is low, a walk, a bike ride, a swim, yoga or a dance class can lift it. A regular wind-down before bed can help with sleep.
move.why: Reviews of more than 1,000 trials find that exercise improves mood, and walking, yoga and strength training do especially well. In a review of 15 trials, women who exercised also reported fewer premenstrual symptoms.

premenstrual.sources: Singh and others 2023, British Journal of Sports Medicine. Noetel and others 2024, BMJ. Pearce and others 2020, BJGP Open. Bertone-Johnson and others 2005, Archives of Internal Medicine (calcium from food). Thys-Jacobs and others 1998, American Journal of Obstetrics and Gynecology. Wyatt and others 1999, BMJ (vitamin B6). TGA safety alert on vitamin B6, 2023. Baker and Driver 2007, Sleep Medicine.

general.body: Sanguine cannot place this day in a phase with enough confidence, for example when cycles vary a lot or a period is later than expected. These notes hold for any day of the cycle.
general.anyDay: These notes hold for any day of the cycle.

reason.late: Your period is later than the range Sanguine expected (by {date}), so it can't place this day in a phase.
reason.wide: Over your last {n} cycles, lengths have varied from {min} to {max} days, so the middle of your cycle can only be narrowed to {width} days. This day falls inside that stretch, so it isn't placed in a phase.
reason.wideNoRange: The middle of your cycle can only be narrowed to {width} days so far. This day falls inside that stretch, so it isn't placed in a phase.
reason.paused: While {state} is set, Sanguine doesn't estimate the middle of the cycle, so it can't place this day in a phase.
reason.pausedUnnamed: A life state you set in Settings pauses the estimate of the middle of your cycle, so Sanguine can't place this day in a phase.
reason.setAside: This cycle was left out of estimates ({quality}), so its days aren't placed in a phase.

move.tip: Regular activity on most days, with muscle-strengthening at least twice a week. On low days, even a short walk helps.
move.why: This is Australia's physical activity guideline. Reviews of more than 1,000 trials find that exercise improves mood and energy.

general.sources: Australian Dietary Guidelines 2013. NHMRC Nutrient Reference Values. Australia's Physical Activity and Sedentary Behaviour Guidelines. Singh and others 2023, British Journal of Sports Medicine. Wender and others 2022, Frontiers in Psychology.

iron.tip: Iron-rich foods, such as red meat, chicken, fish, lentils, tofu or leafy greens, with vitamin C from citrus, capsicum or tomato in the same meal. For example: a beef and broccoli stir-fry, lentil dahl with a squeeze of lemon, or a spinach and chickpea curry with tomatoes.
iron.why: Monthly bleeding is why women aged 19 to 50 need 18 mg of iron a day, against 8 mg for men. Vitamin C in the same meal helps the body absorb iron from plant foods.

omega3.tip: Omega-3 fats from oily fish such as salmon, sardines or mackerel, or from walnuts, chia and linseed. For example: sardines on wholegrain toast, or salmon with greens and rice.
omega3.why: Omega-3 is the fat tested in the period-pain trials, taken as a supplement (see below). Whether eating it as food eases pain is untested; fish twice a week fits general heart-health advice.

vitaminC.tip: Vitamin C from kiwifruit, oranges, strawberries, capsicum or broccoli, alongside iron-rich meals. For example: muesli with kiwifruit and yoghurt, or a chicken and capsicum stir-fry.
vitaminC.why: Vitamin C helps the body absorb iron from plant foods, which helps refill what the period used. No study shows a special need for it in this phase.

bVitamins.tip: Foods rich in B vitamins, especially riboflavin and thiamine, such as milk, yoghurt, eggs, wholegrain cereals, legumes, mushrooms and leafy greens. For example: porridge made with milk, or eggs and mushrooms on wholegrain toast.
bVitamins.why: In a 10-year study of more than 3,000 nurses, women who got the most riboflavin (B2) and thiamine (B1) from food were 25 to 35% less likely to develop premenstrual symptoms. B vitamins from tablets showed no such link, the study only observed, and nobody has tested whether timing in the cycle matters.

zinc.tip: Zinc from beef, chicken, oysters, pumpkin seeds, chickpeas or cashews. For example: a chicken and chickpea salad topped with pumpkin seeds, or a beef burrito bowl.
zinc.why: Zinc helps cells grow and repair, and women need 8 mg a day. In 6 small trials, zinc supplements eased period pain. Nobody has tested whether eating more zinc at this time of the cycle helps.

fibre.tip: Fibre-rich foods such as oats, legumes, vegetables, wholegrains and fruit with the skin on. For example: overnight oats with berries, or a bean and vegetable soup.
fibre.why: Fibre helps the body clear estrogen through the gut, which is the idea behind eating more of it around the estrogen peak. But in a study of 250 women, those who ate the most fibre had lower hormone levels and more cycles without ovulation, so more is not always better. Fibre's everyday benefits for the gut are well established.

vitaminDB6.tip: Foods with vitamin D and vitamin B6, such as oily fish, eggs, chickpeas, potatoes and bananas. For example: a salmon and potato traybake, or a chickpea curry followed by a banana.
vitaminDB6.why: One small study found lower vitamin D and vitamin B6 markers around ovulation. Nobody has yet tested whether eating more of them at this time helps.

protein.tip: A source of protein at each meal, such as eggs, Greek yoghurt, fish, meat, tofu or legumes. For example: eggs on toast, Greek yoghurt with nuts, or a lentil and feta salad. Feeling hungrier in this phase is common.
protein.why: Amino acids, the building blocks of protein, were lower in this phase, and a small study found a higher need for one of them. On average women eat a little more now, in step with a small rise in the energy the body uses at rest.

magnesium.tip: Magnesium from leafy greens, nuts, seeds, legumes, wholegrains and dark chocolate. For example: a handful of almonds, brown rice with black beans, or a spinach and pumpkin-seed salad.
magnesium.why: Women need 310 to 320 mg a day. Small trials of magnesium supplements reported fewer premenstrual symptoms, but studies of magnesium from food are mixed.

b12.tip: Vitamin B12 from meat, fish, eggs and dairy, or from fortified plant milks and nutritional yeast if you eat a plant-based diet. For example: a tuna sandwich, or a smoothie made with fortified soy milk.
b12.why: B12 is needed to make red blood cells, and running low causes tiredness. No study links B12 needs to this phase; it is here because it is easy to miss without animal foods.

calcium.tip: Calcium-rich foods such as milk, yoghurt, cheese, calcium-fortified soy drinks, tofu set with calcium or canned salmon with the bones. For example: yoghurt with fruit, a cheese and salad sandwich, or a tofu stir-fry.
calcium.why: In a 10-year study of more than 3,000 nurses, women who got the most calcium from food were about 40% less likely to develop premenstrual symptoms, and in a trial of 466 women calcium eased them more than a placebo did. Calcium also supports bone health at every age.

carbs.tip: Regular meals with slow-digesting carbohydrate, such as oats, brown rice, wholegrain bread, sweet potato or legumes. For example: a sweet potato and black bean bowl, or wholegrain toast with peanut butter.
carbs.why: Cravings for carbohydrate are common before a period. Regular wholegrain meals are a common suggestion for steadier energy and mood, but few trials have tested it.

zinc.tip: Zinc: in 6 small trials with 739 women, zinc supplements eased period pain.
zinc.why: A 2024 review pooled the trials. Doses varied widely; one trial gave 40 mg of zinc sulfate a day to 103 high-school students. More than 40 mg a day over a long time can lower copper levels.

ginger.tip: Ginger: in small trials, ginger powder taken in the first 3 to 4 days of the period eased period pain.
ginger.why: A 2024 review of 24 studies found less pain than with a placebo and no clear difference from anti-inflammatory pain relievers. Trials used 750 to 2,000 mg of ginger powder a day. The trials were small and their results varied.

omega3.tip: Omega-3 (fish oil): taken daily for 2 to 3 months, it eased period pain in small trials.
omega3.why: A 2024 review of 12 studies with 881 women found less period pain with 300 to 1,800 mg of omega-3 a day. Reviews disagree on how large the effect is.

calcium.tip: Calcium: in one large trial, a daily calcium supplement eased premenstrual symptoms. Calcium-rich foods count towards the same amount.
calcium.why: The trial gave 1,200 mg of calcium a day for three cycles to 466 women. Symptom scores fell more than with a placebo, though the placebo group also improved, and a maker of calcium products helped fund it.

b6.tip: Vitamin B6: small trials for premenstrual symptoms show mixed results. B6 can damage nerves, sometimes at under 50 mg a day: stop and see a doctor if you feel tingling, burning or numbness.
b6.why: A review of 9 trials found some benefit, but the trials were of poor quality. Since 2023 the TGA has required a nerve warning on products with more than 10 mg a day. Several products can contain B6, also listed as pyridoxine, so check every label.

magnesium.tip: Magnesium: a few small, older trials reported fewer premenstrual symptoms; reviews call the evidence limited.
magnesium.why: The trials had 28 to 38 women each, and another study found no benefit. Studies comparing blood magnesium in women with and without premenstrual symptoms are inconclusive.

nextPeriod.legend95: About 19 in 20 within the whole bar
nextPeriod.a11y: 8 in 10 chance it starts between {lo80} and {hi80}; about 19 in 20 between {lo95} and {hi95}
nextPeriod.thisDayA11y: This day, {day}, is marked on the bar.

ovulation.title: Ovulation and fertile window

curve.band: The shaded band is the likely range for ovulation.
curve.labelExtras: LH (luteinising hormone) peaks briefly around the middle; FSH (follicle-stimulating hormone) is highest early; body temperature steps up a little in the second half.

ovulation.stripOvulation: ovulation estimate days {lo} to {hi}, most likely day {point}
ovulation.stripFertile: fertile window estimate from day {lo} to day {hi}

how.label: HOW IT WAS WORKED OUT
how.periodEndNone: There are no earlier periods to go on yet, so a typical length is used and the range is wide. It narrows as you log more.
how.periodEndFew: A few periods are not much to go on, so the range is wide. It narrows as you log more.
how.periodEndPicture: Typical period length is up to 8 days. Yours: {list}.
how.periodEndShaded: Shaded: periods up to 8 days long are within the typical range used by gynaecologists worldwide.
how.nextPeriodNone: You have no completed cycles yet, so this rests on what a study of 612,613 cycles found: cycles averaged 29.3 days, and two in three were 25 to 30 days long.
how.nextPeriod: Your own cycles ({count} used) are combined with what a study of 612,613 cycles found: cycles averaged 29.3 days, and two in three were 25 to 30 days long. Together they point to a cycle of about {mean} days for you.
how.nextPeriodFew: With only {count} of your cycles, the study still carries much of the weight. After about six regular cycles your own pattern takes over and confidence can reach high.
how.calendarOnly: Worked out from your period dates only: no ovulation tests or temperatures this cycle
how.ovulationCalendar: The phase after ovulation lasts about 12.4 days on average, and Sanguine allows give or take 2.6 days for it, so ovulation is placed that far before your expected next period.
how.ovulationCalendarWide: Cycles differ mostly in the phase before ovulation, so an estimate from period dates alone can be several days off. Positive ovulation tests or a temperature rise would narrow it.
how.ovulationPast: This cycle has ended, so the estimate uses its known length instead of a forecast.
how.fertile: The fertile window is the 6 days ending on ovulation day.
how.fertileWide: Because ovulation itself is uncertain, the green band spreads wider, darker on the days most likely to be in the window.
how.src1: Munro and others 2018, International Journal of Gynecology and Obstetrics (FIGO bleeding ranges).
how.src2: Bull and others 2019, npj Digital Medicine (612,613 cycles, 124,648 users).
how.src3: Wilcox and others 1995, New England Journal of Medicine (221 women).
